divisions.question: The majority voted in favour of an [amendment](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2008-11-12.91.1) introduced by Liberal Senator [George Brandis](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/queensland/george_brandis), who explained that: > *The purpose of the opposition’s amendment is to ensure that the provisions of this act, when it receives royal assent, come into effect retrospectively, as from 1 July 2008—in other words, the commencement of the current financial year—and that, in the event that there are some individuals who, as a result of the reference to the Senate committee, might have been prejudiced because of the death of a partner to whom the provisions of the bill would otherwise have applied, then the position of anybody in that unfortunate circumstance can be secured.* ### What does this bill do? This bill was introduced to amend the fourteen Acts governing and regulating [superannuation](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superannuation_in_Australia) schemes in order to increase coverage of same-sex couples and their children. It comes following [Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission's](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_and_Equal_Opportunity_Commission) report [Same Sex: Same Entitlements](https://www.humanrights.gov.au/same-sex-same-entitlements). Read more about the bill in its [bills digest](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/billsdgs/86LR6/upload_binary/86lr66.pdf;fileType=application/pdf).

speeches.speaker: John Faulkner
speeches.brief: The bills were introduced together, with a motion to proceed without formalities and be read a first time, which was agreed to.

speeches.speaker: John Faulkner
speeches.brief: The speech introduced bills to implement the Montreal Convention for international air carrier liability, strengthen Customs border enforcement and search powers, modernise customs procedures, define tobacco content for duty, and amend the Export Market Development Grants scheme. Key changes include removing the air liability cap with claims up to 100,000 SDR (about A$172,000), and raising the EMDG maximum grant to $200,000, the turnover limit to $50 million, and lowering the expenditure threshold to $10,000.

speeches.speaker: Chris Ellison
speeches.brief: The opposition moved to refer several government bills to Senate committees for extended inquiry, arguing they required careful scrutiny and were not election policies. The government accused the opposition of economic vandalism, claiming the delays would cost up to $284 million and undermine the budget surplus strategy.
The debate resumed on the luxury car tax bills, with an amendment moved by Senators Bartlett and Nettle to require passage by 24 June 2008 and to omit paragraph (2) of the motion.

speeches.speaker: Joe Ludwig
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the opposition is delaying eight bills through Senate committee referrals without proper justification, including the Same-Sex Relationships (Superannuation) Bill 2008 and the Commonwealth Electoral Amendment (Political Donations and Other Measures) Bill 2008. The speaker urged the opposition to support the same‑sex superannuation bill by 1 July, and to pass electoral reforms lowering the donation disclosure threshold to $1,000, banning overseas and anonymous donations, and preventing parties from profiting from public funding.

speeches.speaker: Glenn Sterle
speeches.brief: The Legal and Constitutional Affairs Committee report on the Same-Sex Relationships (Equal Treatment in Commonwealth Laws—Superannuation) Bill 2008 was presented and ordered to be printed.

speeches.speaker: George Brandis
speeches.brief: The opposition supported the Same-Sex Relationships (Equal Treatment in Commonwealth Laws—Superannuation) Bill 2008 and related bills to end discrimination against same‑sex couples, citing the principle of equal treatment and noting that about one million Australians identify as homosexual; the speaker also expressed disappointment with the government’s late tabling of 18 pages of amendments.

speeches.speaker: Sarah Hanson-Young
speeches.brief: The government argued that the Same-Sex Relationships (Equal Treatment in Commonwealth Laws—Superannuation) Bill 2008 removes discrimination against same-sex couples and their children in Commonwealth superannuation schemes, and announced amendments to reinstate marriage references and adopt a new definition of 'child' from the Family Law Act. The bill does not require private superannuation funds to recognise same-sex relationships but facilitates it, and the speaker urged the opposition to pass the bill without further delay.

speeches.speaker: Penny Wong
speeches.brief: Senator Brandis argued that the superannuation bill should be backdated to 1 July 2008 to protect same-sex partners who died after that date, citing the opposition's earlier proposal by Mr Turnbull; the government opposed, citing legal complexities and offering ministerial discretion for ex gratia payments, and the amendment was defeated.

speeches.speaker: Penny Wong
speeches.brief: The speaker moved the third reading of the Same-Sex Relationships (Equal Treatment in Commonwealth Laws—Superannuation) Bill 2008, congratulating the government for removing many discriminatory laws against same-sex couples but criticising both major parties for failing to end marriage discrimination. They stated the Greens would continue to advocate for full equality, including marriage, and acknowledged bipartisan support for the bill's passage.

The House of Representatives returned the bill with amendments, agreeing to Senate amendments (2), (3) and (4) but disagreeing to amendment (1) and proposing further amendments. The proposed changes include compensating individuals who lost payments under specified Acts or trust deeds due to delayed commencement, with the Finance Minister required to determine full compensation upon application.

speeches.speaker: Nick Sherry
speeches.brief: The government moved to accept the House of Representatives' alternative amendment to the bill, rejecting the Senate's retrospective amendment from 1 July 2008 due to legal complications and constitutional concerns. The opposition accepted the government's amendment, noting it now provides an enforceable right to full compensation for lost superannuation payments, achieving effective retrospectivity.
